case_name: CASE OF KHAGHAGHUTYAN YERKKHOSUTYUN v. ARMENIA

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant NGO, which operates an online database monitoring fatalities and crimes in Armenia’s armed forces for the purpose of advancing human rights and transparency (see paragraph 6-7), faced repeated refusals by the Ministry of Defence to disclose requested data on soldier deaths, including names, dates, and causes (see paragraphs 8, 10, 11, 13-14). The Administrative Court ultimately upheld the Ministry’s refusal, preventing the NGO from accessing the information (see paragraphs 18, 20, 22). This refusal to provide information constitutes a clear interference with the applicant’s right to receive and impart information under Article 10 of the ECHR, as the NGO’s work involves the dissemination of public-interest data critical to its mission (see paragraph 16). Thus, an interference with Article 10 exists.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference was grounded in domestic law. The Ministry of Defence cited multiple legal provisions as the basis for its refusal, including Article 23 of the Constitution (right to privacy), Article 201 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (secrecy of investigative information), sections 8(1) and 9 of the Freedom of Information Act, sections 2, 8(3)(c)-(d), and 12 of the State and Official Secrets Act, Government Decree no. 173, and the Minister of Defence’s Order no. 9-N (see paragraphs 11, 15, 18, 22, 24, 29, 35-39). While the Constitutional Court later ruled that certain provisions of the State and Official Secrets Act (notably section 12(7)) were unconstitutional for overly broad classification practices (see paragraph 40), the domestic legal framework at the time of the interference provided a sufficient basis for the restriction, as it was accessible, foreseeable, and relied upon by the domestic courts (see Antar and Others v. Turkey, no. 22768/12, § 38). Therefore, the interference was lawful.
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued legitimate aims under Article 10(2). The Ministry of Defence and domestic courts justified the refusal on the grounds of national security, citing the military-political context and the need to protect combat capability (see paragraphs 15, 17-18, 20). National security is a recognized legitimate aim under Article 10(2). Additionally, the classification of the requested data as a state secret under the State and Official Secrets Act invoked the protection of information that could undermine military security (see paragraph 35), which also aligns with the aims of preventing disorder and protecting national interests (see paragraph 12(7) of the Act and Kenedi v. Hungary, no. 30457/06, § 42). Thus, the interference served legitimate aims.
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference fails the necessity test. While the domestic authorities invoked national security as a justification, the reasons provided were generic and lacked concrete evidence that disclosure of the requested fatalities data would pose a *real and pressing* threat to national security. The NGO sought information on peacetime fatalities (e.g., accidents, crimes) to address human rights issues such as corruption and impunity in the armed forces—a matter of significant public interest (see paragraphs 6, 13, 16). The ECtHR has consistently held that restrictions on access to information of public interest, particularly concerning human rights, require *relevant and sufficient* reasons to justify the interference (see Magyar Helsinki Bizottság v. Hungary, no. 48876/08, § 160; Társaság a Szabadságjogokért v. Hungary, no. 37374/05, § 36). Here, the Ministry’s bare reference to national security and combat capability (see paragraphs 17-18, 20) was insufficient, especially given that (i) the Ministry had previously disclosed similar data for 2010-2011 without apparent harm (see paragraph 9), (ii) the NGO’s request pertained to historical, non-operational data, and (iii) the classification was imposingly broad, covering all fatalities-related information retroactively via Order no. 9-N (see paragraph 39). The lack of a tailored, proportionate assessment of the specific risks (see speak Stoll v. Switzerland [GC], no. 69698/01, § 106) means the interference cannot be considered *necessary in a democratic society*.
